entries.what_happened: One manuscript, 'The Falconer distance conjecture in all dimensions' (OpenAI, dated September 23, 2026), is the whole family. Its abstract and main theorem (Theorem thm:main, section 00_introduction) say: for every integer d ≥ 2 and every compact E ⊂ ℝᵈ with dim_H E > d/2, the distance set Δ(E) = {|x−y| : x, y ∈ E} has positive Lebesgue measure, L¹(Δ(E)) > 0. The proof (sections 02–10) takes two separated Frostman probabilities on compact subsets of E, builds decreasing pair filters Γ_N, and approximating distance measures τ_N whose Fourier mass on dyadic shells decays by a power (Proposition 'shell-decay'). A monotone-measure reconstruction lemma then gives a nonzero absolutely continuous limit carried by Δ(E) (Lemma 'monotone-shell', Proposition 'completion'). In odd dimensions an angular projection gain (section 03_angular_gain) and a thin-tube upgrade (Proposition 'thin-upgrade') supply the half-dimension needed; the classical Falconer threshold argument handles the case where the measure charges an affine plane.
entries.delivers: The unpinned positive-measure statement for compact sets: for every d ≥ 2 and every compact E ⊂ ℝᵈ with dim_H E > d/2, L¹(Δ(E)) > 0. This covers d = 2 and every d ≥ 3. The text says it imposes no regularity beyond compactness and the strict dimension inequality (no Ahlfors regularity, equal packing and Hausdorff dimension, product structure or Fourier decay), and that the distances are measured in the original space. The abstract and the text say this resolves the Falconer distance conjecture. Against the list's wording, the claim matches clause (a) (every integer d ≥ 2), clause (c) (positive Lebesgue measure of the distance set) and the strict inequality. It restricts clause (b) from 'sets' to 'compact sets': the introduction restates the conjecture for compact sets and the theorem assumes compactness. The text does not treat non-compact or non-Borel sets and gives no reduction from such a set to a compact subset of the same dimension.
entries.remains: If the claim holds, nothing is left open for compact sets with dim_H E > d/2 in any dimension d ≥ 2. Not covered by the text: (i) sets that are not compact (Borel, analytic or arbitrary sets), which the list's bullet does not exclude; (ii) the endpoint dim_H E = d/2, which the introduction says is 'not asserted'; (iii) the pinned version, where the text says it makes no claim about a single pin at the threshold d/2.
entries.direction: proves the conjecture for compact sets
entries.conditional_on: Yes. The odd-dimensional case (d = 2k−1, k ≥ 2) uses the planar discretized Furstenberg estimate (Theorem ang:furstenberg, stated without proof). The manuscript takes it from Orponen–Shmerkin (OS2023, Theorem 1.3), in the tube formulation of Orponen–Shmerkin–Wang (OSW2024, Definitions 2.5–2.6 and Theorem 2.7), and section 03 calls it 'the only deep input'. The manuscript's claim is conditional on that published theorem being correct as stated. Standard facts (Frostman's lemma, Mattila's Fourier identities, Folland and Simon measure theory) are used without proof. The radial L^p lemma (prep:radial-lp) is adapted from Orponen 2019, but its proof is written out in section 04. OpenAIDistinctDistances2026 is cited only as context in the introduction and is not used in any proof step.
entries.doubts: (1) The introduction's own history gives Wolff's 4/3 as the best unpinned planar threshold for positive measure. It gives Liu 2026 as a planar result only for Borel sets whose Hausdorff and packing dimensions are equal, and Guth–Iosevich–Ou–Wang's 5/4 only for a pinned conclusion. The manuscript claims the unpinned planar statement for every compact planar set with dim_H E > 1. The claim is therefore well beyond the thresholds the text itself cites, and the text supports it only with its own argument. (2) In several places the text asks the reader to repeat an earlier argument rather than writing it out: the second-endpoint bound in the restoration-of-mass lemma (asm:retained-measures) holds 'with the endpoints reversed'; the integer-cap lemma (prep:integer-caps) says 'repeat with α and β interchanged'; and the negative-shell bound follows 'the same' way. (3) The final shell inequality comes from a long chain of parameter choices (β, κ, σ, ω, T) with error terms absorbed into 'the stated losses'. The text leaves some of these steps to the choices, for example 'increasing the starting N if necessary'.
